Cognitive dissonance is psychological tension associated with a perceived conflict among a person's beliefs, attitudes, actions, or other cognitions. In Leon Festinger's theory, the tension can motivate a person to change a belief or action, add a justification that makes the elements fit together, or reduce the importance of the conflict.

Leon Festinger's A Theory of Cognitive Dissonance (1957) set out a framework for relations among cognitions: they can be consonant, dissonant, or irrelevant. The theory connects the discomfort of dissonance with pressure to reduce it; the strength of that pressure depends in part on how important the conflicting cognitions are.

Festinger and James M. Carlsmith tested a forced-compliance prediction in a 1959 study. After participants did a tedious task, some were paid to tell the next participant it had been enjoyable. Participants given a small payment later rated the task more positively than those given a larger payment. The authors interpreted the smaller reward as providing less external justification for the statement, leaving greater pressure to resolve the inconsistency.

The theory helps explain why people may revise a belief, reinterpret evidence, or change behavior when their own commitments and actions feel at odds. The response depends on the situation; inconsistency alone does not predict one uniform reaction.

Cognitive dissonance names a proposed psychological process, not a synonym for disagreement, hypocrisy, or being mistaken. A conflict between two people does not establish that either person is experiencing dissonance.

In learning and teaching, the idea can help describe tension between a person's commitments about education and what they observe in practice. It does not by itself settle what a good response to that tension should be.

A complex situation contains many interacting parts whose relationships produce emergent behavior: outcomes arise from how the whole behaves, not only from summing the parts.

Cause-and-effect is often opaque beforehand and becomes clearer in retrospect (“hindsight sensemaking”); useful progress usually blends direction with experimentation and feedback, not a single fixed blueprint.

The term appears in everyday speech (“this is complex”) and in systems thinking (complex adaptive systems), organization theory, and frameworks such as the Cynefin framework, where complex marks the domain of novel emergence and probe–sense–respond leadership patterns—contrasted with Compli/cat/ed domains where analysis and expertise can yield a knowable best approach.
Complex does not simply mean “large” or “messy”; a huge but tightly constrained workflow can be complicated rather than complex in the technical sense.
Non-linear coupling — Small changes can have disproportionate effects; effects can feed back through multiple pathways.
Path dependence — History matters; similar-looking starts can diverge because prior interactions shape what is possible next.
Emergence — Macro patterns (norms, accidents, performance cliffs, cultural dynamics) arise from micro interactions and constraints.
Epistemic humility — Multiple plausible explanations can coexist until you intervene and observe what actually happens in this context.
Complex — Expect surprise in kind, not only in quantity of detail; interventions are often hypotheses to be tested and revised.
Compli/cat/ed — Expect difficulty in degree: intricate, but often analyzable into components with stable enough rules that expertise can predict outcomes and recommend a strong approach.

Overlap in practice — Real systems mix both qualities (complicated interfaces sitting atop complex socio-technical dynamics); labeling helps choose methods (analysis vs iterative probing), not to pretend the world is only one or the other.
Complex — Organizational change where incentives, trust, and tooling interact; traffic and urban dynamics; ecosystems and markets with adaptive actors.
Misleading usage — Using “complex” as a synonym for “I don’t want to explain it” blurs the distinction; prefer naming what is uncertain (unknown constraints, political coupling, feedback loops).
Something complicated has many parts, dependencies, or steps, so it can feel difficult or expensive to work with—but the underlying situation is still knowable and analyzable in principle.
With enough expertise, time, and decomposition, you can often trace causes, predict outcomes, and apply a right answer or a good procedure (even if discovering it was painful).

The word is casual English (“this deployment is complicated”) and also technical in sensemaking frameworks (for example the Cynefin framework), where complicated names the domain of known unknowns resolved by analysis and good practice, contrasted with Complex situations where cause and effect emerge and are clearer only after the fact.
Complicated work can still be hard; the distinction is not “easy vs hard” but decomposability and predictability of the system’s behavior under study.
Decomposition — Subproblems can be separated, owned, and reasoned about with expert judgment and established methods.
Legibility — With enough mapping, the system’s structure and interaction rules can be made explicit (diagrams, contracts, runbooks).
Optimizable — There is often a meaningful sense of better vs worse designs once constraints and goals are stated.

Complicated — Relationships are intricate but often stable enough that experts can forecast what will happen when you change X; surprises tend to come from scale, detail, or missing information, not from novel emergence every time you intervene.

Complex — Many interacting forces produce emergent behavior; the same intervention can land differently depending on history and context; useful knowledge is often built through probing, feedback, and safe-to-fail experiments, not a single exhaustive blueprint.

Practical heuristic — If the hard part is doing all the work carefully, it may be complicated. If the hard part is that the situation keeps teaching you something new when you touch it, it may be complex.
Complicated — A large but well-specified migration with many moving parts; tuning a known performance model with many knobs; a dense legal agreement where experts can still say what clauses imply.
Not automatically complex — “Many components” alone does not imply Complex; a complicated assembly line can still be mostly predictable if interactions are constrained and monitored.
